narrative:
The model estimates there’s a 19 % chance you won’t pass your final year, which is above the 10 % threshold that triggers extra support. That’s why you’re being asked to take remedial courses.

The three factors that mattered most in this estimate were your past school record, why you chose this school, and your plans after graduation. Because you’ve never failed a class before, the model sees that as a strong positive sign—it’s actually pulling your risk down. On the other hand, the fact that you picked this school mainly for its reputation rather than the course itself is nudging the risk up a bit. Your clear intention to go on to higher education is another positive signal, again lowering the predicted risk.

Other aspects of your situation also played a role. Your family relationships are rated as very bad, which is quite different from most students who report good or very good relationships, and this pushes the risk higher. You also don’t have internet at home, which is unusual—90 % of your peers do—and that too raises the estimate. On the positive side, you study between two and five hours a week, which is about average, and you’ve had no absences, so those factors don’t add to the risk.

The remedial courses are designed to give you extra time and support in the subjects that need it most. Use this opportunity to build a consistent study routine, reach out to teachers or counselors if family stress is getting in the way, and explore free internet options at school or the local library so you can access online resources.
